event.description: Frances Loeb Library Faculty Author Talk Please join us in the library for a conversation between Hannah Ahlblad and Jorge Otero-Pailos on Treaties on De-Fences. Treaties on De-Fences is an artist book of prints created by Jorge Otero-Pailos and made available to the public on the occasion of his 2024 Park Avenue sculptures exhibition Analogue Sites. Much like the exhibition, the artist’s book of prints aims to raise awareness and advocate for the preservation of modernist U.S. embassies. While the art installation uses large sculptures, as a method to make these embassies visible and tangible to the general public, the artist's book of prints further enacts and intertwines the energy of the sculptures and the diplomatic treaties from which the sculptures derive their names. This event is free and open to the public. Participants are invited to attend in person in the Loeb Library or join via livestream, here. This event will be recorded.
event.title: Treaties on De-Fences

event.description: About artists' books. What defines an artist’s book? Why create one, and how do you bring one to life? Join us on Tuesday, September 15 for Archives Party #25 in Special Collections to learn directly from Jorge Otero Pailos the ins and outs of producing his Treaties on De-Fences. If you’re curious: it focuses on the US Embassy in Oslo by Eero Saarinen (built 1959, now decommissioned) and how it offered a space for the reframing of a preservation intervention. Other artist’s books from our collections will be on exhibit as well. Bring your curiosity, interest, and questions! This event is co-hosted by Special Collections from the Frances Loeb Library and Jorge Otero Pailos. Please join us this Tuesday, September 25 at 6:00 pm in Special Collections! Registration opens Monday, September 14 at 10 am.
event.title: Archives Party 025: About artists' books.

event.description: Hannah Greenwald Healy - Harvard University The rate of infectious disease outbreaks is increasing globally and in the U.S. due to factors like international travel, climate shifts, and declining vaccination rates. Environmental surveillance— the systematic testing of water or air for health-relevant markers— can complement clinical surveillance infrastructure, often providing early warning and more comprehensive data on infectious disease trends. In this talk, Dr. Healy will describe the resurgence in wastewater surveillance during the COVID-19 pandemic and her work since then to advance the technology and expand to new targets. Next, she will discuss how environmental monitoring and cleaning practices can reduce exposures to waterborne pathogens in healthcare environments. Finally, she will discuss her lab’s work on expanding the utility of wastewater surveillance to unsewered settings, including communities in the Peruvian Amazon. Together, these studies demonstrate how environmental surveillance can support infectious disease management through water system management, infection prevention, and public health response. Hannah Greenwald Healy has been an Assistant Professor of Environmental Health and Exposure Science at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health since January 2025, where she runs the Healy Health ‘Omics (H2O) Lab. She holds a secondary appointment in the Department of Environmental Science and Engineering and is Associate Faculty at the Broad Institute. Dr. Healy is trained as an Environmental Engineer, receiving her B.S. from Georgia Tech and M.S. and Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to her faculty appointment, she completed a Gaylord Donnelley Postdoctoral Fellowship at Yale University in the Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering. Her research group at Harvard aims to improve public health by monitoring and controlling pathogens and their broader microbiomes in water systems.
event.title: Environmental surveillance for managing infectious disease outbreaks locally and globally

event.description: Amy Kyungwon Han (Associate Professor, Seoul National University) Soft robotics enables safe and adaptive interaction with humans, delicate objects, and dynamic environments through compliant actuators, sensors, and mechanisms. This talk presents the design and application of soft robotic technologies for haptics, gripping, and medical applications, with an emphasis on compact, low-power, and application-specific solutions. Examples include an origami-based haptic device for remote manipulation, hybrid electrostatic mechanisms for handling deformable objects with reduced gripping force, and soft cardiac assistive technologies designed to operate under physiological constraints. Through these examples, the talk highlights how mechanism design and system integration can address challenges in actuation, sensing, safety, and compatibility, demonstrating the potential of soft robotics for safe and adaptive interactions across haptics, gripping, and medical applications. Bio: Amy Kyungwon Han is an Associate Professor of Mechanical Engineering at Seoul National University. She was a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford and received a Ph.D. and M.S. from Stanford and a B.S. from Georgia Tech. Her research includes soft actuators, sensors, medical robotics, haptics, and manipulation. Prof. Han's awards include the MIT Technology Review Innovators Under 35 Asia Pacific, 50 Women in Robotics, Rising Star of RoboSoft, ICRA New Generation Star, and Best RA-L Paper Award. event.description: 2026 Barbara Grosz Distinguished Lecture in AI and Society Title: AI's Models of the World, and Ours Speaker: Jon Kleinberg, Tisch University Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Information Science at Cornell University Abstract: When we see someone performing at the top of their craft, we often marvel both at their observable achievements and the hidden, internal expertise that they've accumulated. Something similar is true with generative AI and large language models (LLMs): their successes involve both powerful observable behavior as well as deep internal representations of the world that they construct for their own uses. How do these internal representations work, and how similar or different are they compared to the representations of the world that we build as humans? This distinction is becoming crucial as people interact with powerful AI systems, where a mismatch between the system's model of the world and our human models of the world can lead to situations in which the system inadvertently `sets us up to fail' through our interactions with it. We explore these questions through the lens of generative AI, drawing on examples from game-playing, geographic navigation, and other complex tasks: When we train a model to win chess games, what happens when we pair it with a weaker partner who makes some of the moves? When we train a model to find shortest driving routes, what happens when it has to deal with unexpected detours? The picture we construct is further complicated by theoretical results indicating that successful generation can be achieved even by agents that are provably incapable of identifying the model they're generating from. The talk will include joint work with Ashton Anderson, Karim Hamade, Reid McIlroy-Young, Siddhartha Sen, Justin Chen, Sendhil Mullainathan, Ashesh Rambachan, Keyon Vafa, Fan Wei, Chris Qiu, and Prabhakar Raghavan. event.description: Engineering materials are selected for fixed properties and then protected with safety factors, because repeated loading degrades them. Living structural materials do the opposite: bone senses mechanical loading and converts it into mineral deposition where stiffness is needed, while coral self-stiffens as waves cement its skeleton. This talk asks whether synthetic materials can likewise use mechanical loading itself as the signal that improves them and presents two complementary routes toward that goal. The first route grows material in response to load. Cyclic loading of piezoelectric scaffolds in an electrolyte generates surface charges that drive mineralization in proportion to stress. The resulting composites gain both stiffness and energy-dissipation capacity under the very cyclic loading that would normally fatigue them, and the growth is self-limiting, with a saturation thickness set by the applied force. Recent results show that force also controls the nucleation density, crystallization kinetics, and hardness of the mineral, pointing to mechanical energy as a general lever for directing crystallization. The second route architects the response to load. Lattices built from liquid crystal elastomers couple snap-through buckling of tilted beams with the rate-dependent soft elasticity of mesogen rotation. The result is a reusable energy-absorbing metamaterial whose dissipation rises with strain rate by a power law and reaches densities comparable to those of plastically deforming metals. Together, these results outline a path toward structural materials that adapt, reinforce, and protect autonomously, with implications ranging from orthopedic implants and marine structures to protective equipment and soft robotics. event.description: Paolo Decuzzi (Italian Institute of Technology and Stanford University) The therapeutic performance of drug delivery systems can be enhanced by tailoring the geometrical and mechanical properties of the carrier itself. This lecture explores this idea through two microstructured drug delivery platforms: μMESH, designed for the local treatment of tumors, and μPL (microPLates), developed for the management of osteoarthritis. μMESH is a flexible, biodegradable film that conforms to irregular biological surfaces, establishing close contact with residual tumor margins and favoring a more uniform distribution of therapeutic agents within the tumor microenvironment. Its unique geometry, with two distinct compartments, enables the controlled and independent release of very different therapeutic molecules. Across different glioblastoma models, both immunosuppressive and immunoresponsive, these features lead to substantial improvements in survival. A similar concept has driven the design of μPL for the treatment of osteoarthritis. These are 20 μm square plates engineered to be retained within the leaky synovial cavity and to boost the interaction with the cartilage surface. In particular, hyaluronic acid μPLs, by deforming at the cartilage interface and reducing friction, protect against mechanical wear while serving as local therapeutic depots. Together, these two examples suggest that the geometrical and mechanical features of drug delivery systems can synergize with the activity of the therapeutic molecules, enhancing the overall efficacy. Dr. Paolo Decuzzi is a Senior Scientist and Professor of Biomedical Engineering at the Italian Institute of Technology in Genoa, Italy, where he founded the Laboratory of Nanotechnology for Precision Medicine in 2015. He earned an M.Sc. in Mechanical Engineering from the Polytechnic University of Bari, Italy, and completed his Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering at the University of Naples – Federico II in 2001. event.description: UNLEASHING THE DUENDE : A talk and embodied workshop with Alfredo Minetti & Fernanda Ghi What is duende? Poet Federico García Lorca described it as a raw, embodied creative force that overtakes a performer — not skill, not style, but an expressive drive that arrives only through vulnerability and risk. This 2-hour event explores that question first through ideas, then through the body. Cultural anthropologist and pianist Alfredo Minetti opens with a short talk on why genuine artistic risk has become so rare in performance today. Drawing on Lorca, Guy Debord's Society of the Spectacle, and Neil Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death, he traces how consumer culture and entertainment saturation have pushed the performing arts toward spectacle and surface polish, sidelining the vulnerability that makes performance feel alive. Using classical concert music as a case study — including pianist Glenn Gould's defiant breaks from convention — Minetti makes the case for reclaiming performance as something lived and risked, not simply produced and consumed. Minetti and choreographer Fernanda Ghi then engage in a conversation on these ideas, bringing together their perspectives as musician and dancer before moving into direct physical experience. Ghi leads participants into that embodied exploration: Is duende an energy? An emotion? A force that wakes the most authentic, creative self? Through guided breathing, free movement, and improvisation — both solo and with a partner — participants will explore what happens when the body moves beyond learned technique and habit. The practice invites letting go, releasing control, quieting the analytical mind, and simply being present — creating the conditions for duende to emerge. event.description: Under current government and corporate AI leadership, many of us feel discouraged or powerless. But if we take strategic action together, we have the power to bring AI under public control and determine how it’s used, how it’s regulated, and who it benefits. Historically, action from just 3.5% of the population has tipped the scales and always led to serious political change (known as the 3.5% rule). This workshop series provides opportunities for participants to shape AI policy through collective civic action. During times of difficulty pushing for federal action, states serve as an important powerhouse for policy leadership, sandboxing, and resistance. In this workshop, we will engage in 3 Massachusetts campaigns taking action against unsafe, unregulated, and undemocratic AI: Policy leadership – Massachusetts is now pioneering legislation with the strongest AI regulation language in the country (Amendment 471). This campaign aims to pass the amendment. Resistance against undemocratic AI adoption – In February 2026, Gov. Maura Healey made Massachusetts the first state to roll out ChatGPT across the entire executive branch, with citizens getting no say. This campaign aims to demand transparency and citizen oversight. Resistance against pre-emption – Massachusetts Rep. Lori Trahan drafted a bill that would preempt state AI laws for three years. This campaign aims to get Trahan to drop the bill. Please join us to learn more and contribute your voice and action. RSVP for lunch
